title: Edge adapter primitives and rollback matrix
content:
Purpose: quick draft of a lightweight adapter/shim strategy for VPC/IAM/Cluster primitives that lets us evolve module interfaces with minimal customer friction and a deterministic rollback story. This is intentionally pragmatic: small modules + explicit signal resources + an importer helper script rather than a big sweeping refactor.

Background/context:
- We frequently need to change outputs (naming), add optional resources (eg secondary route tables, nodegroup role attachments), or split monolithic primitives into smaller pieces to support on-prem and cloud parity.
- Existing approaches in the repo either (a) break downstream state during rename, or (b) rely on heavy migration PRs per customer. We need a pattern that:
  * preserves backward compatibility by default,
  * makes deprecation explicit and reversible,
  * has a testable, automatable migration path for upgrades.

Proposal summary (high-level):
1) Introduce an "edge-adapter" primitive module per domain: network-adapter, iam-adapter, cluster-adapter. Each adapter sits between the consumer primitive (tenant module) and the infrastructure primitive (vpc, iam, eks). Adapters expose the old contract (outputs/vars) and map to the new primitives.
2) Use a small set of "signal" outputs and shadow resources to maintain state continuity: signal resources are lightweight terraform-managed resources (tags, null_resource with trigger, or a tiny aws_ssm_parameter) whose stable identifiers we can use for imports/mapping during the upgrade.
3) Provide an importer helper (python/Go CLI) that reads both old and new state mappings and performs safe terraform state mv/imports and prints a rollback plan. This avoids manual per-customer sed/grep in statefiles.
4) Versioning and deprecation policy: semver with major-only-breaking-changes; adapters are a short-lived compatibility shim with a maximum lifecycle of 3 months after the publicized deprecation date.

Adapter module responsibilities (details):
- Variables:
  * accept both new and legacy input names (eg vpc_id and legacy_vpc_id) and prefer explicit new vars when present.
  * provide a single boolean var "adapter_force_migration" for customers who opt-in to automatic state migration (default false).
- Outputs:
  * export legacy output names exactly (for downstream existing modules) as well as normalized outputs new modules will consume (eg vpc.id -> vpc_id_legacy and vpc_id).
  * add an "adapter_migration_signal_id" output (stable string) used by the importer script to correlate resources.
- Resource mapping:
  * do not recreate/replace underlying infra by default. Instead use data sources to look up existing resources when an explicit migration is requested.
  * when creating new resources, emit a small aws:ssm or gce metadata entry tagged with the adapter_migration_signal_id to make future discovery easier.

State migration strategy:
- Non-destructive path: adapter_module introduced, which reads legacy outputs via data/terraform_remote_state or by referencing existing resources. No state moves. Downstream consumers continue to see legacy outputs.
- Assisted migration path (recommended for seatwide upgrades): run importer helper with --dry-run, which will:
  1) fetch state for target workspace and new module workspace,
  2) compute minimal set of terraform state mv + import operations,
  3) emit a terraform plan snippet and a reverse (rollback) snippet,
  4) optionally apply state moves when --apply is provided.
- Emergency rollback: if --apply performed state moves, the importer writes a rollback plan file and stores it as artifacts (GH PR/CI). The adapter module keeps old outputs exported until the rollback plan TTL expires.

Rollback/compatibility matrix (examples):
- Scenario A: rename output vpc_id -> vpc_id_external
  * Adapter approach: adapter exports both vpc_id (legacy) and vpc_id_external (new). No state change. When ready, run importer to move downstream references to new output (state mv of references) and then remove legacy export in next minor.
- Scenario B: split single cluster module into cluster-core + cluster-nodegroups
  * Adapter maps legacy cluster id to cluster-core.id. Nodegroups are created under new module. Use signal resources to ensure existing nodegroup IAM bindings are preserved. Importer will import nodegroup resources into new module state blocks.
- Scenario C: add new required var (eg cidr_allocations) that cannot be inferred
  * Provide adapter var backfill tooling (cli prompts + dry-run); set default conservative values and emit explicit warnings. Strongly prefer marking as optional and scheduling a major bump if inference impossible.

Testing & CI checklist:
- Local integration harness: small k8s/e2e terraform test that deploys upstream (legacy) stack, introduces adapter, runs importer --dry-run, verifies outputs remain identical to callers.
- Golden-state tests: check-in small statefiles to test harness for common patterns (rename, split, optional var add).
- Canary workflow for hosted private-deploy customers: rollout adapter on a small subset of accounts/workspaces and verify non-regression metrics (cluster join, node readiness, healthchecks).

Operational runbook (short):
- Pre-upgrade: run importer --dry-run; review suggested state-mv list; open PR with state-mv patch and rollback plan attached.
- Apply window: prefer low-traffic windows; perform state moves first, then apply terraform changes.
- Post-upgrade verification: run smoke tests, confirm downstream callers resolve intended outputs; monitor for 24–72 hours.
- Rollback: run rollback script produced by importer; if terraform state has drifted, escalate to SRE & use provider-specific export/import tooling.

Open design decisions / TODOs:
- Should adapters write an explicit aws:ssm parameter or prefer tag-only signals? SSM is more discoverable but adds IAM surface area.
- Decide whether adapter modules live in the same mono-repo as primitives or a separate compatibility repo to limit churn.
- Build importer as a small go CLI (fast, static binary) vs python (easier iteration).

Notes to reviewers (quick):
- This is intentionally conservative: avoid changing customer resource IDs. The goal is to avoid resource replacement and minimize manual state surgery.
- The importer is the only place we will perform terraform state mv/import operations; it must be idempotent and produce explicit rollback artifacts.

Next steps (short roadmap):
1) Prototype network-adapter for a single VPC rename + add secondary-route-table change. 2) Build importer --dry-run proof-of-concept. 3) Run internal canary on staging accounts and iterate.

Appendix (example commands):
- importer dry-run: ./tf-adapter-importer --workspace=customer-123 --module=network-adapter --dry-run
- apply migration: ./tf-adapter-importer --workspace=customer-123 --module=network-adapter --apply --auth-profile=redwood-ops

Rough acceptance criteria for graduating adapter out of draft:
- importer dry-run accuracy > 99% on golden states, documented rollback file created for every apply, and at least two successful canary migrations in staging.

End of draft.

Quick TODO list (short bullets):
- [ ] pick signal resource type (SSM vs tag)
- [ ] spike importer prototype (go)
- [ ] prototypical adapter for vpc rename case
- [ ] CI golden states check-in
- [ ] write confluence explainer and change timeline

Comments welcome; ping @Marco / @Priya for infra/iam edge cases.
